This article continues [Citing a Set of Tables](citable-sets.html): same set,
same bucket. Run it before that article's teardown. The set was written in R;
here a Python program reads it, for example to serve it from an API.

The Python reader is the [`datom` package on PyPI](https://github.com/amashadihossein/datom-py).
It only reads.

## Install

Python 3.10 or later:

```sh
pip install "datom[s3]" keyring
```

`[s3]` adds S3 support. `keyring` is not part of datom; it holds the keys here,
as it does in the R articles.

## Credentials

datom never looks for credentials. AWS environment variables, `~/.aws/` and
instance roles are all ignored. You pass a function that returns the keys, and
datom calls it when it needs them. Store the keys once in the OS keychain:

```sh
keyring set study001 aws_access_key_id
keyring set study001 aws_secret_access_key
```

```python
import datom
import keyring

def study001_keys():
    return {
        "access_key": keyring.get_password("study001", "aws_access_key_id"),
        "secret_key": keyring.get_password("study001", "aws_secret_access_key"),
    }
```

With AWS single sign-on, `datom.sso_credentials("my-profile")` makes the
function for you; run `aws sso login --profile my-profile` first.

## Read the set

```python
store_liver_safety = datom.store_s3(
    "study001", prefix="liver-safety/", region="us-east-1", credentials=study001_keys
)
conn_liver_safety = datom.get_conn(store_liver_safety, project_name="study001-liver-safety")

x = datom.get_set(conn_liver_safety, "study001-liver-safety")
x
#> DatomSet(name='study001-liver-safety', project='study001-liver-safety', version='35e39f62', members=6)
```

That is version 3, written after the refresh. `version="d2d0456b"` reads version
1. Reading a set fetches no member data.

## Fetch a member

```python
liver_flags = datom.fetch_member(conn_liver_safety, x, "liver_flags")
```

`liver_flags` is a pandas data frame at the version the set pins, `0f89dd1b`,
not whatever is current.

The inputs live in the imported project, so they need their own connection, as
in R:

```python
store_imported = datom.store_s3(
    "study001", prefix="imported/", region="us-east-1", credentials=study001_keys
)
conn_imported = datom.get_conn(store_imported, project_name="study001-imported")

lb = datom.fetch_member(conn_imported, x, "lb")
```

Fetching `lb` through `conn_liver_safety` stops, naming the project `lb`
belongs to.

## Behind an API

A small [FastAPI](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/) app serving `liver_flags`:

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI, Response

SET_VERSION = "35e39f62"   # the version your report cites

x = datom.get_set(conn_liver_safety, "study001-liver-safety", version=SET_VERSION)
liver_flags = datom.fetch_member(conn_liver_safety, x, "liver_flags")

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/version")
def version():
    return {"set": x.name, "version": x.version}

@app.get("/liver-flags")
def get_liver_flags():
    return Response(liver_flags.to_json(orient="records"), media_type="application/json")
```

The pin keeps the API serving what the report cites, even after someone writes
version 4. A pinned version never changes, so reading it once at startup is
safe. To move the API, change the pin and restart.

This app has no authentication: anyone who can reach it can read the data. Put
access control in front of it before exposing it.

## What Python checks

The same checks as R, before handing over any data: the document's format
version, that a set is a set and a table a table, that the version asked for
matches exactly one, and that the downloaded bytes match their recorded hash.
A failed check raises a `datom.DatomError` whose `code`, such as
`integrity_mismatch`, says which.

Not yet:

- **Writing.** Tables and sets are written in R.
- **Governance lookup.** Python reads from the bucket and prefix you give. If
  the project has governance attached, it warns that the location may move.

S3 support is a preview. The [datom-py README](https://github.com/amashadihossein/datom-py#readme)
has the details.
